To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) explicit instruction on and extensive practice with the phonology of words (form focused instruction) has more positive effects on vocabulary, phonological processing, and letter knowledge compared to explicit instruction on and minimal practice with the semantics of words (meaning focused instruction), (b) the ability to learn word pairs that differ minimally in their phonological form is a good predictor of vocabulary and phonological awareness gain in children who receive form-focused instruction, and (c) the ability to distinguish word pairs

(a) explicit instruction on and guided practice with word form during interactive storybook reading has a stronger impact on phonological awareness and letter name knowledge than does meaning-focused instruction, (b) both types of instruction are equally effective in increasing children's receptive vocabulary, and (c) explicit instruction on word form during interactive book reading is particularly effective in increasing children’s knowledge of word meanings when the children are good at discriminating words that sound similar

form-focused vocabulary instruction had a greater impact on semantic and phonological knowledge of target vocabulary than meaning-focused vocabulary instruction, and that learners who had greater ability to learn pairs with minimal acoustic- phonetic differences showed greater gain in semantic knowledge and letter knowledge after form-focused vocabulary instruction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of literacy skills in young children.
the question of how to teach vocabulary in the early school years.
the development of literacy abilities, with particular emphasis on vocabulary knowledge, in young children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the form of the words is important for learning the meaning of the words.
the form-focused instruction is better than the meaning-focused instruction.
the form of words is a crucial factor for the development of vocabulary, phonological skills, and letter knowledge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a focus on the form and meaning of words during instruction has different effects on young learners’ vocabulary development, phonological awareness and letter skills.
form-focused instruction is a promising way of supporting children's early literacy development.
the more you know about the form of a word, the better you can learn about it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the form-focused approach to vocabulary instruction should be considered for use in the classroom.

the phonological form and the semantic knowledge of a word are not necessarily acquired together and that it is important to explicitly teach the meaning and the phonological form in a coordinated fashion.

form-focused instruction can be used as an effective instructional strategy to improve vocabulary development, phonological awareness and letter recognition in young children. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
